passages.title: Questions 111–115
passages.body: When Elizabeth Long began investigating women's book groups in the mid-1980s, her research plan provoked two profoundly different sets of reactions. Women, who had themselves participated in such groups, as well as men whose mothers and grandmothers had done so, immediately grasped the importance of her project : "You will never know what a difference it made" was the phrase she heard again and again. But among her academic colleagues, common readers seemed to be occupying a zone of cultural invisibility. They were not of interest to literature departments, whose major focus is on books and authors, not readers. They were not of interest to sociologists or political scientists because women's reading groups do not pursue activities with any obvious relationship to formal political processes. Long, however, went on to show that such groups had mobilised the women's suffrage and Progressive movements at the grassroots. Scholars of popular culture had not found reading groups interesting because the groups read canonized fiction and did not transform their cultural consumption into a 'resistant' subcultural style. It had not yet occurred to them that the so-called highbrow canonical literature could be immensely popular and devilishly subversive. David Vincent's Bread, Knowledge and Freedom (1981) had already demonstrated the important role of reading in inspiring working-class consciousness in early nineteenth-century Britain. As a sociologist, Long concluded that the really important question that needed answering was why academics did not care about readers.
passages.source: CDS II 2026 English set A (set code BFVS-F-GNE – A)

passages.title: Questions 116–120
passages.body: Christopher Columbus of Spain set foot in the New World in 1492. Six years later, Vasco da Gama of Portugal reached India. During the next two centuries the Spaniards and the Portuguese actively transferred, not only to Europe but to many parts of Asia as well, a number of plant species which they encountered in South and central America, in expectation of their potential either as food or as medicine. These plants had been developed to a high degree by the Maya and Inca civilizations of these regions. Of these, the potato (Solanum tuberosum) is believed to have been domesticated in terraced slopes on the high plateau of Bolivia-Peru in South America, sometime between 5000 and 2000 BC. Europeans first saw potatoes in South America in 1537, and around 1570 a Spanish ship brought the first potatoes to Europe. Though termed papa in South America, they were incorrectly called batata (the name for the sweet potato) when John Gerard first described them in English in 1597, and this name stuck. An 1860 report states that by 1780, potatoes, peas and beans were in high repute as foods in Calcutta, and that the Dutch are said to have been the first to introduce the culture of potatoes, which was received from their settlement of the Cape of Good Hope. From there the British received annually the seeds of every kind of vegetable useful at the table, as well as several plants of which there appears to be much need, especially various kinds of pot herbs.

questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: In a typical Indian village today, one is certain to find groups of women talking about finance.
S6: In a society where women play significant but never-recognised roles, being a part of an SHG which gives them such financial power is indeed a matter of pride.
P: Sitting there, they might proudly introduce themselves by saying that they are members of a self-help group (SHG).
Q: Alternatively, they might lend money at reasonable interest rates to members for starting small businesses.
R: They can be seen sitting under a tree, in an abandoned school building, or in the front yard of a village resident's dilapidated home, holding thick notebooks.
S: An SHG is usually a community group of 10-12 women from similar socio-economic background who pool their financial resources for taking up joint economic activities.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Scene-setting, then explanation.
Step 1: S1: groups of women talk finance in villages. R: where and how they sit (under a tree, with notebooks).
Step 2: P: 'Sitting there' they introduce themselves as SHG members. S defines SHG. Q: 'Alternatively' they lend money.
Step 3: S6 sums up pride in SHG.
Answer: (b) RPSQ.

Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: For much of history, surnames, or last names, were not considered necessary.
S6: These two pieces of medieval bureaucracy meant that virtually everyone had to settle on a definite and fixed surname.
P: The other was the enactment of the Statute of Additions in 1413, which required that all legal documents to contain not just the person's given name, but also his or her occupation and place of abode.
Q: One was the introduction of a poll tax in 1379, which led the government to collect the name of every person aged sixteen or over.
R: But sometimes, the process was accelerated such as in England where two events gave a boost to the adoption of surnames.
S: The business of acquiring surnames was a long one that evolved over centuries rather than years.
questions.explanation:
Concept: General statement, exception, example.
Step 1: S1: surnames were once unnecessary. S: getting surnames took centuries.
Step 2: R: 'But sometimes' faster, as in England, two events. Q: 'One' (1379 poll tax). P: 'The other' (1413 statute).
Step 3: S6 'These two pieces' refers back to Q and P.
Answer: (d) SRQP.

S1: In 1984, two small clay tablets of vaguely rectangular shape were found in Tell Brak, Syria, dating from the fourth millennium BCE.

S6: It was only after major restoration work was carried out to restore the pond's storage capacity that the community could return to its traditional livelihood.

Q: However, overexploitation caused the pond to shrink to half its original size and reduced its water storage capacity by 60 per cent.
R: The pond, spread across 2.4 hectares, supported irrigation, sustained the fishing community, met household needs and remained home to a wide variety of flora and fauna.

questions.explanation:
Concept: Past use, decline, result.
Step 1: S1: pond was the main source. R: pond's size and uses.
Step 2: Q: 'However' overexploitation shrank it. S: as it disappeared people used groundwater. P: groundwater level dropped 'as well'.

S6: This is something the Impressionist artists were able to master and it gave a shimmering, lively quality to many of their paintings.

Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: Circadian rhythm is a term used to refer to the physical, mental and behavioural changes an organism experiences over a 24-hour cycle.
S6: Maintaining a good circadian rhythm through appropriate exposure to natural light, consistent sleep schedules and times of eating, and adequate physical exercise during the day can allow an organism to live a healthy life.
P: Prolonged disruption, moreover, can cause long-term damages such as metabolic diseases, cardiovascular problems, and mental health issues.
Q: Light and dark (daytime and night-time) have the biggest influence on these circadian rhythms.
R: Circadian rhythms are also affected by food intake, stress, physical activity, social environment and temperature.
S: When any one or more than one of these cause the circadian rhythm to be disrupted, it can lead to sleep problems, drowsiness and poor focus.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Main factor, other factors, disruption, long-term damage.
Step 1: S1 defines circadian rhythm. Q: light and dark influence it most. R: 'also affected' by food etc.
Step 2: S: when 'any of these' cause disruption, sleep problems. P: prolonged disruption causes long-term damage. S6: maintain a good rhythm.
Answer: (b) QRSP.

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: All the different parts of our eye help us to see.
S6: These electrical signals then travel through the optic nerve to the brain which in turn converts these signals into the images we see.
P: The iris, which is the coloured part of the eye, controls how much light the pupil lets in.
Q: Next, light passes through the lens, the clear inner part of the eye, which focuses this light on the retina.
R: First, light passes through the cornea, the clear front layer of the eye, and enters the eye through an opening called the pupil.
S: When it hits the retina, special cells called photoreceptors convert the light into electrical signals.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Follow the path of light.
Step 1: R: First, cornea and pupil. P: iris controls light into the pupil. Q: Next, lens focuses on retina. S: on the retina photoreceptors convert light to signals.
Step 2: S6 continues with the optic nerve.
Answer: (d) RPQS.

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: Humans in colder climates first began wearing some form of sturdy foot covering at least 40,000 years ago.
S6: Today, minimalistic barefoot shoes are becoming popular because they allow the wearer to feel the ground beneath their feet while still offering some protection and support.
P: Unfortunately, modern shoes have also had a negative impact on feet due to bad design such as a narrow toe box, difference in heel to toe drop, however slight, and stiff soles.
Q: Earlier skeletons had very robust little toes that could bend and grip surfaces.
R: These gradually evolved to become less substantial than the big toe because shoe-like coverings reduced the mechanical stress on them and made them weaker.
S: The evidence for this comes from the study of changes in the structure of the toe bones of foot skeletons from that time.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Evidence, finding, change, modern problem.
Step 1: S1: shoes began 40,000 years ago. S: 'The evidence for this' comes from toe bones.
Step 2: Q: earlier skeletons had robust little toes. R: 'These' gradually weakened. P: 'Unfortunately' modern shoes harm feet.
Step 3: S6: barefoot shoes today.
Answer: (a) SQRP.
